claims.text: The baseline is an equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy produced under standard processing conditions.
The baseline equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy has moderate lattice distortion.
Widening atomic-size mismatch by changing Al content or adding a minor element will increase local lattice distortion.
Increasing local lattice distortion stabilizes a single-phase structure in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
Enhanced local lattice distortion creates a rough energy landscape.
Enhanced local lattice distortion increases the density of stable grain boundaries.
Higher lattice distortion hinders long-range atomic diffusion.
Higher lattice distortion equilibrates the mobilities of vacancies and interstitials.
Equilibrating vacancy and interstitial mobilities suppresses defect clustering.
Suppressed diffusion and defect clustering reduce the nucleation and growth of secondary phases.
The proposed increase in lattice distortion will help retain high-temperature strength.
The proposed increase in lattice distortion will help retain environmental resistance.
The proposed increase in lattice distortion will help retain radiation tolerance.
The proposed increase in lattice distortion will help retain cryogenic toughness.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will contain fewer or finer secondary precipitates.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will accumulate fewer irradiation-induced defects, including fewer or no dislocation loops.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will have superior mechanical properties under high-temperature, irradiated, and cryogenic conditions.
The hypothesis is applicable to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys and similar systems having moderate baseline lattice distortion.
The quantitative effect of increased lattice distortion on defect recombination and phase stability is not yet established.
Grain-size variation and residual stresses may also affect the measured outcomes.
